text: Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
this morning I posted a video about the
translation of Genesis 1:1. And I had a
wonderful question posted in one of the
comments sections. They said, "What is
the source of the light in Genesis 1:3
if God created the sun in day four?" And
this is more intriguing if you look at
the fact that starting in day one, you
have evening and morning and very
clearly divided days. So, what is the
source of that light? Well, this is
something that has plagued commentators
for a long time because it doesn't make
much logical sense. But there are a
couple of possible ways to resolve
what's going on here. See, if we look at
the six days of creation, there is a
poetic symmetry to what's going on. The
first three days of creation see these
environments being created, light and
dark, waters above, waters beneath,
waters in dry land. The next three days
of creation see the inhabitants of those
environments created. Parallel to day
one, day three sees the celestial bodies
created. Parallel to day two, day four
sees the fish of the sea and the birds
of the sky, which is kind of the space
that is left by the firmament that uh
separates the waters above from the
waters beneath. Day six corresponds to
day three where we have the inhabitants
of the dry land. And so this poetic
symmetry seems to be taking precedence
over logical consistency. And so if we
think that they knew that the sun was
the source of the light that
distinguished the day from the night, we
would expect them to have the sun be the
source of that light. But if they're
putting this poetic symmetry where we
have the environment and then the
inhabitant of the environment created in
the second set of three creative days,
then maybe they're just not worried
about that logical consistency. And so
really the poetry and the artistry is
what takes priority. And this would be
one of the reasons not to understand
this as a literal creation account that
the authors and the earliest audiences
would have understood to be asserting
the actual physical way that the
universe was created. Now, another way
to understand it is to imagine that they
did think the light and the dark came
from some other source besides the sun
and that the sun and the moon were just
these lights that happen to inhabit the
day and the night without actually
causing them. And there are some
scholars who think that may be what's
going on. And if you imagine that light
is the very first emanation from God,
the very first creation of God and that
God is ultimately the sustainer of that
light, then maybe God is the one who is
responsible for the distinction between
the day and the night. And then in day
four, you just have the sun and the moon
as the great lights that are inhabiting
those periods that are established
independently of those celestial bodies.
That's another way to understand what's
going on. And that takes a little more
seriously the idea that this creation
account was intended to represent a
literal description of how the actual
universe was thought to have been
created by the authors and the earliest
audiences of these texts. Uh we know
that the six creative periods are
supposed to be 24-hour days because they
fit with the description of the evening
and the morning how they understood the
days to cycle in that time period. And
so the notion that these are creative
periods that extend beyond 24 hours is
not really supported by much. But me
personally, when I look at what's going
on here, I tend to think that the poetic
symmetry there, the artistry of the six
creative periods is probably taking
priority over any notion that this is a
literal strict description of what
actually took place when the universe
was created. And I think it's probably
because this is a lurggical text. This
was probably intended for use in temple
ceremonies or in New Year's festivals or
something like that. And as I've
discussed many times before, the
creation account in Genesis 1, the
priestly creation account, is intended
to revise and correct and supersede the
earlier creation account in Genesis 2
that featured a number of elements that
the priestly authors obviously didn't
like. And so I don't think they
understood this as a literal description
of how the universe was physically and
actually created. I think they
understand it as a literary creation and
something that is propaganda, something
that is dogmatic but not necessarily
tied to a literal understanding of the
creation of the universe so much as
ideologies regarding how we want to
understand
uh the nature and the origins of the
universe from a dogmatic point of view
rather than from like a scientific or a
historical point of view. So, I tend to
think the artistry, the poetry is just
taking priority here. But that's
certainly not the only way to understand
this passage. But hopefully that helps.
And the fit for this video has been
Thundercats.
